title: Central Valley GNSS sites did not rebound in wet 2023 as GRACE storage recovered; 2021-2022 drought subsidence equalled 2014-2015 at equal storage deficit (20 sites, 2007-2026)
abstract: Question: did the land surface of California's Central Valley rebound when GRACE water storage recovered in the wet 2023 water year, and did drought subsidence per unit storage deficit change between the 2012-2016 and 2020-2022 droughts? Approach: we used Nevada Geodetic Laboratory IGS20 daily vertical positions at 60 valley-floor GNSS stations (2004-2026), measured the September-October height change for each water year, removed a regional common mode from 22 stable stations, and compared the results with CSR GRACE/GRACE-FO mascon storage and the CDEC San Joaquin Valley index. Results: the common mode followed the GRACE storage change (r = -0.90), so it is an elastic water-load signal of about -8 mm in wet years. GRACE valley storage recovered 117% of its 2019-2022 loss in water year 2023. At 17 subsiding sites the median load-corrected height change in 2023 was -11 mm (95% interval -46 to +1 mm); 4 sites went up and 11 went down; the best site recovered 20% of its 2020-2022 subsidence. Subsidence continued in 2024-2026 (medians -33, -16 and -18 mm per year; no site went up). At equal GRACE deficits (-13.0 and -13.4 cm), the 2021-2022 rate equalled the 2014-2015 rate at the same site (median ratio 1.00, 0.93-1.15, 15 sites). A storage-level model fitted to 2008-2019 predicted 2020-2022 subsidence (median obs/pred 1.13, uncertain); a runoff-index model under-predicted it. Limitations: GNSS sites are points and do not give subsidence volume, several records end in July 2025, step corrections are approximate at fast sites, GRACE includes snow and surface water, and two droughts cannot separate SGMA from other causes; the 2024-2026 hint of less subsidence than the model predicts is not clear.
